claim: Intraperitoneal BCG administration results in heterologous protection against Salmonella Typhimurium in the spleen.
source: Relative to the control group, mice that received BCG exhibited enhanced protection against S.Tm, with a four- to fivefold decrease in CFU, indicating TI-mediated splenic protection.
evidence: Demonstrated by CFU measurements showing 4-5 fold reduction in S.Tm load in BCG-trained mice compared to controls (Figure 1B).

claim: BCG vaccination causes expansion of the myeloid compartment in the spleen.
source: We observed an overall expansion of the myeloid compartment due to training, with an increase in the CD11b+ subset, and a pronounced reduction of resident RPM (Figure 1D).
evidence: Flow cytometry data showing increased CD11b+ cells and decreased RPM in BCG-treated mice.

claim: BCG training induces a subset of classical monocytes marked by CXCL9 expression (CM-T).
source: We identified a subset of trained CM (CM-T) particular to BCG (Figure 1G). This subset represents an enhanced state of the STAT1-regulated IFNγ response that characterizes trained CM (e.g. Gbp2, Ly6a, Cxcl9, and Irg1; Figure 1J).
evidence: Single-cell RNA-seq clustering and differential gene expression analysis identified CM-T subset with elevated STAT1-regulated genes.

claim: BCG vaccination causes depletion of resident red pulp macrophages (RPM).
source: We observed an overall expansion of the myeloid compartment due to training, with an increase in the CD11b+ subset, and a pronounced reduction of resident RPM (Figure 1D).
evidence: Flow cytometry measurements showing decreased RPM percentages in BCG-treated mice.

claim: STAT1 and its downstream targets are upregulated across multiple myeloid cell types following BCG training.
source: Stat1 and its downstream targets (e.g. Gbp2, Irf1, and Ly6a), exhibited a pronounced elevation also in other myeloid cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), aligning with an earlier report that BCG induces BM and HSC remodeling via interferon signaling, resulting in STAT1 upregulation in progenitors (Kaufmann et al., 2018).
evidence: scRNA-seq data showing elevated expression of STAT1 and downstream genes across myeloid populations, supported by prior literature.

claim: SCA-1 (Ly6a) expression is increased across monocyte subsets and mcDC2 following BCG training.
source: We also observed increased SCA-1 (Ly6a/e) expression across the monocyte subsets and mcDC2, most notably in NCM (Figure 1F; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Single-cell RNA-seq data showing elevated Ly6a expression in multiple cell types.

claim: The STAT1 signaling pathway is involved in the regulation of SCA-1 expression.
source: The STAT1 signaling pathway has been shown to be involved in the regulation of SCA-1 expression (Yang et al., 2017), suggesting a role for STAT1 in the modulation of SCA-1 during development of TI.
evidence: Cited literature demonstrating STAT1 regulation of SCA-1.

claim: SCA-1+ monocytes exhibit a pro-inflammatory phenotype during infection.
source: Recent studies have also demonstrated a link between SCA-1 and inflammation, with its expression found to be upregulated on a specific subset of Ly6C+ monocytes during infection (Biram et al., 2022). These SCA-1+ monocytes exhibited a pro-inflammatory phenotype, characterized by the production of inflammatory cytokines and chemokines, and were implicated in the amplification of these responses.
evidence: Cited literature showing pro-inflammatory characteristics of SCA-1+ monocytes.

claim: BCG training downregulates CCR2, S100A8/9, and NGP in trained classical monocytes.
source: In addition to the upregulation of inflammatory and antimicrobial genes, we also observed a significant downregulation of specific genes in CM-T as a result of training, including Ccr2, S100A8/9, and Ngp (Figure 1J).
evidence: Differential gene expression analysis showing reduced expression of these genes in CM-T.

claim: IFNγ-induced downregulation of CCR2 is mediated by mRNA instability.
source: CCR2, a chemokine receptor crucial for monocyte recruitment, was found to be downregulated in response to IFNγ. This reduction in CCR2 expression is mediated by IFNγ-induced mRNA instability, potentially serving to retain monocytes at the site of recruitment and dampen a positive feedback loop (Penton-Rol et al., 1998).
evidence: Cited literature describing mechanism of CCR2 downregulation by IFNγ.

claim: Protection against S.Tm persists for 2 months post-BCG vaccination but wanes over time.
source: Notably, protection against S.Tm persisted for 2 months post-vaccination, albeit with waning resistance over time (Figure 2B).
evidence: CFU measurements at 14 and 60 days post-vaccination showing reduced but persistent protection.

claim: BCG is not detected in the bone marrow following intraperitoneal administration.
source: While intravenous (i.v) BCG delivery and subsequent localization of the bacterium to the BM were previously noted as crucial for robust training (Kaufmann et al., 2018; Khan et al., 2020), our results indicate that during i.p administration this process is dispensable, as no BCG were detected in the BM (Figure 2C).
evidence: CFU measurements from bone marrow showing no detectable BCG across all time points.

claim: BCG is detected in the spleen at all time points following intraperitoneal administration, with CFU declining sharply by day 14.
source: Conversely, in the spleen, we isolated BCG at all time points, with CFU declining sharply by day 14, reaching the limit of detection by day 30 with minimal bacterium remaining (Figure 2C).
evidence: CFU measurements from spleen showing BCG presence and decline over time.

claim: Classical monocytes (CM) are rapidly recruited to the spleen starting at day 3 after BCG, peaking at day 14.
source: Compared to mean control values, we observed rapid recruitment of CMs in the spleen, starting already at day three after BCG, peaking at day 14 before returning to baseline (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Flow cytometry analysis showing temporal dynamics of CM populations.

claim: CXCL9+ classical monocytes (CM-T) reach peak levels at day 14 post-BCG vaccination.
source: We also stained cells for CXCL9 expression, as a marker gene of STAT1-mediated TI that defines the CM-T subset, and revealed that this population reaches peak levels at day 14 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Flow cytometry data showing temporal dynamics of CXCL9+ CM-T population.

claim: CM-T subset shows significant increase already at 5 days post-BCG vaccination.
source: In a separate experiment to assess early kinetics of CM-Ts, we measured a significant increase of this subset already at five days post BCG (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), indicating an early recruitment of these cells due to the initial response to BCG.
evidence: Flow cytometry measurements at day 5 showing elevated CM-T levels.

claim: SCA-1 expression in NCMs persists and remains highly elevated at all time points after day 14.
source: NCMs express SCA-1 (Ly6a), another STAT1-regulated gene, which persists and remains highly elevated at all subsequent time points (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Flow cytometry data showing sustained SCA-1 expression in NCMs over 60 days.

claim: S.Tm challenge at day 14 triggers expansion of CM-Ts, but this response is lost by day 60.
source: Challenge with S.Tm at day 14 triggered an expansion of CM-Ts, but this response was lost by day 60, coinciding with the diminished protection observed at this later timepoint (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Flow cytometry data showing CM-T response to S.Tm challenge at different time points.

claim: SCA-1 expression in NCMs remains upregulated even at day 60 post-BCG vaccination following S.Tm challenge.
source: In contrast, SCA-1 expression in NCMs remained upregulated (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Flow cytometry data showing sustained SCA-1 expression in NCMs after S.Tm challenge at day 60.

claim: RPM loss is evident after 14 days of BCG training.
source: Notably, the expression of STAT1-mediated TI markers is not solely restricted to BM-derived myeloid cells but also occurs in tissue-resident RPM. RPM loss is evident after 14 days of training (Figure 2D), together with increased expression of the STAT1-regulated CXCL9 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: Flow cytometry data showing decreased RPM percentages at day 14.

claim: RPM express increased levels of CXCL9 following BCG training.
source: Notably, the expression of STAT1-mediated TI markers is not solely restricted to BM-derived myeloid cells but also occurs in tissue-resident RPM. RPM loss is evident after 14 days of training (Figure 2D), together with increased expression of the STAT1-regulated CXCL9 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: Flow cytometry data showing elevated CXCL9 expression in RPM.

claim: The greatest transcriptional changes due to BCG training occur at days 14 and 30.
source: Examination of all differentially expressed genes (DEGs) between BCG and PBS across these time points revealed the greatest transcriptional changes at day 14 and 30 (Figure 2E; Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: Bulk RNA-seq analysis showing number and magnitude of DEGs at different time points.

claim: At day 14, BCG training enriches for IFNγ response, IFNα response, and IL6-JAK-STAT signaling pathways.
source: At day 14, we detected enrichment for IFNγ response, IFNα response, and IL6-JAK-STAT signaling, with many genes shared across these pathways (Figure 2F).
evidence: Gene set enrichment analysis of bulk RNA-seq data at day 14.

claim: The STAT1-dependent program includes upregulation of Gbp gene family, Ifitm3, and Socs3 at day 14.
source: This STAT1-dependent program includes several interferon-regulated genes upregulated at day 14, including the Gbp gene family, Ifitm3, and Socs3 (Figure 2G).
evidence: Bulk RNA-seq data showing expression patterns of these genes.

claim: GBPs are guanylate-binding proteins involved in antimicrobial activity and inflammasome activation.
source: GBPs are guanylate-binding proteins involved in antimicrobial activity and inflammasome activation (Tretina et al., 2019), while IFITM3 is an interferon-induced transmembrane protein that plays a role in the antiviral response (Clement et al., 2022).
evidence: Cited literature describing GBP function.

claim: IFITM3 is an interferon-induced transmembrane protein that plays a role in the antiviral response.
source: GBPs are guanylate-binding proteins involved in antimicrobial activity and inflammasome activation (Tretina et al., 2019), while IFITM3 is an interferon-induced transmembrane protein that plays a role in the antiviral response (Clement et al., 2022).
evidence: Cited literature describing IFITM3 function.

claim: SOCS3 blocks IL-6 signaling to allow TNF and IL-12 signaling, which is necessary for mycobacterial infection control.
source: SOCS3, a suppressor of cytokine signaling, particularly via IL-6/STAT3, is a necessary component for mycobacterial infection control. By blocking IL-6 signaling, SOCS3 allows for TNF and IL-12 signaling to occur, initiating CD4-dependent IFNγ release (Carow et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited literature describing SOCS3 mechanism in mycobacterial infection.

claim: IRG1 induction requires bacterial phagocytosis and activation of the TLR-2/MYD88/NFKB axis.
source: For example, Irg1 upregulation is limited to day 14 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G) returning to control values for all subsequent time points. This may reflect that IRG1 induction requires bacterial phagocytosis and activation of the TLR-2/MYD88/NFKB axis (Bomfim et al., 2022).
evidence: Temporal expression data combined with cited literature on IRG1 induction mechanism.

claim: CXCL9 expression increases by day 3, plateaus at day 14, and decreases by day 30.
source: Conversely, an increase in Cxcl9 expression is already observed by day 3, plateauing at day 14, and decreasing by day 30, mirroring its induction in CM-Ts in the flow cytometry analysis.
evidence: Bulk RNA-seq data showing temporal expression pattern of Cxcl9.

claim: STAT1 activity shows initial reduction after 2 weeks followed by sustained upregulation for all subsequent time points.
source: Importantly, the IFNγ response mirrored STAT1 activity, showing initial reduction after 2 weeks followed by sustained upregulation for all subsequent time points (Figure 2H), reinforcing their coupled role in mediating the effects of TI.
evidence: Bulk RNA-seq data showing STAT1 expression dynamics over time.

claim: Ly6a (SCA-1) maintains high expression 2 months post-BCG vaccination.
source: Other downstream targets of STAT1, including Ly6a (SCA-1), maintain high expression 2 months post vaccination (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Bulk RNA-seq data showing sustained Ly6a expression at day 60.

claim: Day 30 post-BCG vaccination is characterized by enrichment of E2F targets, G2M checkpoint, and heme metabolism pathways.
source: Distinct from these immune signatures, day 30 was characterized by enrichment of E2F targets, G2M checkpoint, and heme metabolism (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: Gene set enrichment analysis of bulk RNA-seq data at day 30.

claim: RPM play a crucial role in iron homeostasis by recycling and storing iron from senescent erythrocytes.
source: Interestingly, RPM play a crucial role in iron homeostasis, recycling and storing iron from senescent erythrocytes, preventing accumulation of free iron that can lead to ROS production, oxidative damage, and pathogen utilization (Vogt et al., 2021).
evidence: Cited literature describing RPM function in iron homeostasis.

claim: SCA-1 expression in NCMs can be maintained through progenitor programming alone.
source: Within each mouse, we found in the spleen a greater fraction of NCMs expressed SCA-1 from trained donors relative to the naive control (Figure 2—figure supplement 1J). This persistence of the training signature in a naive host environment demonstrates that SCA-1 expression in NCMs can be maintained through progenitor programming alone, though it does not exclude potential contributions of local tissue signals during normal BCG training.
evidence: Bone marrow transplant experiment showing SCA-1 expression in NCMs derived from trained progenitors in naive host.

claim: CM-Ts are undetectable after bone marrow transplant, consistent with the transient nature of this subset.
source: CM-Ts however, were undetectable, consistent with the transient nature of this subset observed in our kinetics data.
evidence: Bone marrow transplant experiment showing absence of CM-T subset.

claim: Approximately 16% of RPM are BM-derived under steady-state conditions.
source: For the majority of RPM, we expected minimal TdTomato expression, representative of self-replenishment during homeostasis. However, already within the control we observed that ~16% of the population were labeled (Figure 3C).
evidence: Lineage tracing data using MS4A3Tdtm reporter mice showing TdTomato+ RPM in control conditions.

claim: BCG training increases the fraction of BM-derived RPM.
source: When this population was depleted during training, an even greater fraction was positively labeled. Accordingly, even under steady-state conditions, BM-derived cells contribute to the resident niche, but when sufficiently diminished post vaccination, active replenishment from the BM does occur.
evidence: Lineage tracing data showing increased TdTomato+ RPM percentage after BCG training.

claim: BCG training increases the percentage of labeled monocytes, suggesting lineage bias towards granulocyte-monocyte progenitors (GMPs).
source: As expected, the monocyte population were primarily double positive (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B). Intriguingly, training increased the percentage of labeled cells across monocytes, suggesting a potential lineage bias towards granulocyte-monocyte progenitors (GMPs).
evidence: Lineage tracing data showing increased TdTomato labeling in monocytes after BCG training.

claim: Training-associated genes are differentially expressed across all sorted cell types including Tdtm+ RPMs, Tdtm- RPMs, and Tdtm+ CM and NCM.
source: Crucially, training associated genes were differentially expressed across all sorted cell types (Figure 3D; Figure 3Figure 1C; Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: Bulk RNA-seq analysis of sorted populations showing DEGs in all cell types.

claim: MHCII-associated genes are enriched in NCM and RPM cells, indicating enhanced antigen presentation.
source: Cluster I is composed of MHCII-associated genes (H2-Aa, H2-Eb1, CD72, etc.), and is enriched in NCM and RPM cells, indicating enhanced antigen presentation that may facilitate the activation of humoral immunity.
evidence: Gene expression clustering analysis showing MHCII gene enrichment in specific cell types.

claim: STAT1-regulated TI hallmark genes including Cxcl9, Gbp2 and Stat1 are upregulated in all trained subsets.
source: Cluster II consists of the STAT-1 regulated TI hallmark genes, including Cxcl9, Gbp2 and Stat1 and is upregulated in all trained subsets.
evidence: Gene expression clustering analysis showing STAT1-regulated genes across cell types.

claim: Genes involved in response to tissue damage and immune infiltration (Aif1, Fpr1, Hk3) are primarily observed in trained RPM.
source: Genes in Cluster III, such as Aif1, Fpr1, and Hk3, are primarily observed in trained RPM and are involved in response to tissue damage/disruption and immune infiltration.
evidence: Gene expression clustering analysis showing specific gene enrichment in trained RPM.

claim: AIF1 is a marker of macrophage activation and is functionally involved in phagocytosis and membrane ruffling.
source: AIF1 is an established marker of macrophage activation and is functionally involved in phagocytosis and membrane ruffling (De Leon-Oliva et al., 2023).
evidence: Cited literature describing AIF1 function.

claim: FPR1 induces chemotaxis, phagocytic uptake, and reactive oxygen species (ROS) production.
source: Similarly, FPR1, a formyl peptide receptor, induces chemotaxis, phagocytic uptake, and reactive oxygen species (ROS) production (Prevete et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited literature describing FPR1 function.

claim: IFNγ response is enriched in CM, NCM, and Tdtm+ RPM following BCG training.
source: GSEA performed across all upregulated genes revealed that the IFNγ response was enriched, followed by IFNα response, allograft rejection, and JAK-STAT signaling (Figure 3F). Although the IFNγ signature was most prominent in CM, it was also observed in NCM and in the Tdtm+ RPM.
evidence: Gene set enrichment analysis of bulk RNA-seq data from sorted populations.

claim: BM-derived RPM maintain a more inflammatory phenotype and heightened sensitivity to IFNγ activation.
source: This finding suggests that engrafted monocytes differentiating within the niche may maintain a more inflammatory phenotype and a heightened sensitivity to IFNγ activation.
evidence: Inference from gene expression data showing stronger IFNγ response in Tdtm+ RPM.

claim: Local tissue-resident RPM also upregulate training-associated genes in response to BCG.
source: However, the BM-derived RPM are not the sole population responsive to training, as the local fraction also upregulates the same genes in clusters I-III.
evidence: Gene expression data showing upregulation of training genes in Tdtm- RPM.

claim: RPM demonstrate a greater capacity to upregulate the expression of many interferon genes, including Cxcl9 and Stat1.
source: Notably, RPM, as a whole, demonstrate a greater capacity to upregulate the expression of many interferon genes, including Cxcl9 and Stat1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Gene expression data comparing interferon gene expression across cell types.

claim: BCG can reprogram populations and generate training via recruitment of trained progenitors and monocytes, and via direct activation of tissue-resident RPM.
source: Taken together, our results indicate that BCG can reprogram populations and generate training via two separate routes. First, the recruitment of trained progenitors and monocytes within the spleen, which differentiate within a vacant niche, retaining their trained identity. Second, activation directly within the spleen in the context of native tissue-resident RPM, generating tissue-specific protection.
evidence: Integration of lineage tracing and gene expression data showing both BM-derived and tissue-resident contributions to training.

claim: STAT1 knockout mice show complete absence of CXCL9 and SCA-1 expression across myeloid populations following BCG vaccination.
source: We observed a complete absence of expression for both CXCL9 and SCA-1 across myeloid populations (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B). This aligns with previous findings that demonstrated compromised acquisition of trained immunity in IFNγR-/- mice (Kaufmann et al., 2018).
evidence: Flow cytometry data from STAT1-KO mice showing no CXCL9 or SCA-1 expression, supported by prior literature.

claim: RPM are preserved in STAT1-KO mice following BCG vaccination, suggesting STAT1-mediated pathways are involved in RPM depletion.
source: Interestingly, RPM, typically depleted following BCG inoculation, remain preserved in STAT1-KO mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that STAT1-mediated pathways are involved in triggering the cellular death processes that occur during BCG interaction and/or engulfment.
evidence: Flow cytometry data showing maintained RPM levels in STAT1-KO mice after BCG.

claim: Fedratinib, a JAK2 inhibitor, blocks STAT1-mediated TI signatures when administered early after BCG vaccination.
source: First, we administered DMSO (control), Deucravacitinib, and Fedratinib i.p followed by BCG or PBS-i.p 4 hr after. These inhibitors were then injected daily via i.p for the following 4 days, followed by a subsequent 9-day rest period (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D). At the 2-week mark, splenocytes were extracted from all mice and analyzed by bulk RNA-seq. Only Fedratinib, not Deucravacitinib, resulted in inhibition of STAT1-mediated TI signatures (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E; Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: Bulk RNA-seq data showing loss of STAT1 signatures with Fedratinib treatment.

claim: Deucravacitinib, a TYK2 inhibitor, does not affect STAT1-mediated TI signatures in the BCG-i.p model.
source: Only Fedratinib, not Deucravacitinib, resulted in inhibition of STAT1-mediated TI signatures (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E; Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: Bulk RNA-seq data showing no effect of Deucravacitinib on STAT1 signatures.

claim: Fedratinib treatment ablates CXCL9+ CM-T population.
source: At the 2-week mark, splenocytes were extracted from all mice for flow cytometry analysis, with CXCL9 utilized as a marker for STAT1-mediated TI signature in CM-Ts. As observed in the transcriptional response, only Fedratinib ablated the CXCL9+ CM-Ts (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Flow cytometry data showing loss of CXCL9+ CM-T with Fedratinib treatment.

claim: Fedratinib treatment suppresses BCG-induced expansion of LSK+ HSCs in the bone marrow.
source: To ascertain this, we isolated BM from the femur, measuring the percent of LSK+ HSCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G). Here too, only Fedratinib resulted in suppressing their expansion to levels comparable to the control (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Flow cytometry data showing reduced LSK+ HSC expansion with Fedratinib treatment.

claim: Early STAT1 inhibition with Fedratinib blocks TI-mediated protection against S.Tm.
source: Importantly, while we observed no differences in CFU between control mice with or without Fedratinib, trained mice receiving Fedratinib were significantly more susceptible to infection (Figure 4B).
evidence: CFU measurements showing loss of protection in BCG-trained mice treated with Fedratinib.

claim: Fedratinib treatment reduces BCG-induced splenocyte expansion and spleen size.
source: Treatment with Fedratinib resulted in diminished recruitment and splenocyte expansion, causing an appreciable reduction in spleen size comparable to the control (Figure 4—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: Spleen size measurements showing reduced expansion with Fedratinib treatment.

claim: Fedratinib treatment shifts monocyte ratios to levels similar to control mice.
source: Accordingly, the balance of monocytes ratios, particularly NCM, was shifted to levels similar to those observed in the DMSO control (Figure 4C).
evidence: Flow cytometry data showing normalized monocyte populations with Fedratinib treatment.

claim: Fedratinib treatment reduces the frequency of CXCL9+ CM-Ts and decreases CXCL9 expression in RPMs.
source: In conjunction, the frequency of CXCL9+ CM-Ts was diminished, reflecting a reduction in the subset, while in RPMs, CXCL9 showed decreased expression (Figure 4D).
evidence: Flow cytometry data showing reduced CXCL9 expression with Fedratinib treatment.

claim: Fedratinib treatment prevents BCG-induced RPM depletion.
source: Finally, RPM, which typically undergo depletion after training, exhibited significantly enhanced survival, similar to the observations in STAT1-KO mice (Figure 4C).
evidence: Flow cytometry data showing maintained RPM levels with Fedratinib treatment.

claim: IFNγ response is the most significantly affected pathway due to JAK2 inhibition by Fedratinib.
source: Analysis of downregulated DEGs identified the IFNγ response as the most significantly affected pathway due to JAK2 inhibition by Fedratinib. This included its downstream effector Stat1, and other key STAT1-regulated trained immunity genes, such as Cxcl9/10, Irf1, Gbp2, and Irg1, across all treated mice (Figure 4E and F; Supplementary file 1e).
evidence: Gene set enrichment analysis of bulk RNA-seq data from Fedratinib-treated mice.

claim: Early α-IFNγ antibody treatment completely ablates STAT1-regulated TI signatures in CM and RPM.
source: Mice were given either α-IFNγ or an isotype control after BCG or PBS vaccination, with injections on days 0, 2, and 4, and assayed 2 weeks post-vaccination. Upon sorting and sequencing CM and RPM from these treated mice, we found that the STAT1 regulated TI signatures were completely ablated with early inhibition (Figure 4—figure supplement 1K–L).
evidence: Bulk RNA-seq data from sorted cells showing loss of STAT1 signatures with α-IFNγ treatment.

claim: Early α-IFNγ treatment does not affect viable BCG levels in the spleen at 2 weeks post-vaccination.
source: Although we measured no changes in viable BCG in cultured spleen homogenates from control and treated mice at the 2-week interval (Figure 4—figure supplement 1M), early α-IFNγ was sufficient in blocking training signatures.
evidence: CFU measurements showing no difference in BCG levels with α-IFNγ treatment.

claim: The acquisition of TI in the tissue occurs within a critically narrow temporal window early after BCG vaccination.
source: Crucially, even though its administration was early and removed after only 5 days administration, inhibition occurred. This indicates that the acquisition of TI in the tissue occurs within a critically narrow temporal window.
evidence: Experimental design showing that 5-day inhibitor treatment is sufficient to block training.

claim: Intraperitoneal BCG vaccination can elicit training without BCG localization to the bone marrow.
source: This leads us to hypothesize that the signaling initiated due to BCG can act in trans, affecting system wide changes, and is not solely acquired due to local pathogen interactions in the BM.
evidence: CFU data showing no BCG in BM but still achieving training and LSK+ expansion.

claim: Training in alveolar macrophages can occur through subcutaneous BCG administration, potentially via the gut-lung axis.
source: Supporting this, recent findings suggest that training in alveolar macrophages can also occur through subcutaneous BCG administration, potentially acting via the gut-lung axis (Jeyanathan et al., 2022).
evidence: Cited literature describing alternative routes of BCG-induced training.

claim: IFNγ-STAT1 pathway is a key driver in establishing trained immunity by replenishment of resident MPs with trained recruited and local immune populations.
source: In summary, our study emphasizes that examining the tissue, specifically the spleen, as a tissue for probing TI offers valuable insights into the temporal dynamics and signaling cascades that instigate and sustain TI locally, in parallel with established systemic effects. Central to these processes is the IFNγ-STAT1 pathway, which we identified as a key driver in establishing TI, by replenishment of resident naïve MPs with trained recruited and local immune populations.
evidence: Integration of all experimental data showing STAT1 requirement for training signatures and protection.

claim: Trained immunity is the capacity of innate immune cells to recall and modulate their subsequent responsiveness following prior exposure to diverse stimuli.
source: Trained immunity (TI) is defined as the capacity of innate immune cells to recall and modulate their subsequent responsiveness following prior exposure to a diverse array of stimuli (Arts et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited definition from established literature.

claim: TI changes are antigen-agnostic and reflect sustained alterations in cellular and systemic states.
source: Unlike the adaptive immune system, these changes are antigen-agnostic and are more reflective of sustained alterations in cellular and systemic states.
evidence: Established characteristic of trained immunity from scientific literature.

claim: TI directly reprograms the metabolic, transcriptional, and epigenetic state of monocytes and macrophages.
source: TI has been demonstrated to directly reprogram the metabolic, transcriptional, and epigenetic state of monocytes and macrophages, generating heightened inflammatory capabilities in-vitro (Arts et al., 2015; Saeed et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited literature describing mechanisms of trained immunity.

claim: The transient lifespans of monocytes and macrophages (weeks only) are insufficient to explain sustained TI protection lasting months to years.
source: As the transient lifespans of these cells are weeks only, this alone is insufficient to explain the sustained protection generated by TI that can last from months to years.
evidence: Logical inference based on cell lifespan and duration of protection.

claim: BCG vaccine facilitates nonspecific protection against heterologous pathogens in mice, primates, and humans.
source: BCG vaccine (Bacillus Calmette-Guérin), an attenuated strain of Mycobacterium bovis, is a potent inducer of TI, which facilitate nonspecific protection against heterologous pathogens in mice, primates, and humans (Darrah et al., 2020; Moorlag et al., 2019).
evidence: Cited literature demonstrating BCG-induced heterologous protection across species.

claim: Intravenous BCG vaccination drives expansion of LSK+ hematopoietic stem cells and multipotent progenitors in the bone marrow.
source: The effects of intravenous (i.v.) BCG vaccination, where bacilli persist within the bone marrow (BM), drive the expansion of LSK +hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) and multipotent progenitors (MPPs; Moorlag et al., 2019).
evidence: Cited literature describing effects of i.v. BCG on HSCs and MPPs.

claim: MPPs undergo biased differentiation towards myelopoiesis following BCG vaccination, increasing proliferation of myeloid cells.
source: In conjunction, MPPs undergo biased differentiation towards myelopoiesis, increasing the proliferation of myeloid cells.
evidence: Cited literature describing BCG effects on progenitor differentiation.

claim: IFNγ and its downstream transcription factors STAT1 and IRF1 drive BCG-induced training in MPPs and short-term HSCs.
source: These effects are driven primarily by interferon activation, particularly that of interferon-gamma (IFNγ) and its downstream transcription factors, STAT1 and IRF1, in MPPs and short-term HSCs, resulting in a transcriptional program of cell cycling (Cdk1, Cdk4, Ccnf) and histone modifications.
evidence: Cited literature describing molecular mechanisms of BCG-induced training in progenitors.

claim: Newly differentiated circulating cells from trained progenitors have enhanced microbicidal properties.
source: Furthermore, these newly differentiated circulating cells have enhanced microbicidal properties (Hasso-Agopsowicz et al., 2024; Qadri et al., 2024).
evidence: Cited literature describing functional properties of cells derived from trained progenitors.

claim: Most tissues harbor long-lived resident macrophages capable of self-renewal, independent of BM-derived precursors.
source: Most tissues harbor long-lived resident macrophages capable of self-renewal, independent of BM-derived precursors. These resident populations, including pulmonary alveolar macrophages, Kupffer cells in the liver and red pulp macrophages in the spleen, originate from embryonic erythro-myeloid progenitors (Kurotaki et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited literature describing origin and characteristics of tissue-resident macrophages.

claim: Resident macrophage niches are repopulated either by self-renewal or by BM-derived progenitors after depletion.
source: Antimicrobial activity of resident populations control early stages of invasion by pathogens but are than depleted, and the niche is repopulated either by self-renewal (Hoeffel et al., 2015) or by progenitors derived from the BM to maintain local functions (Lai et al., 2018).
evidence: Cited literature describing mechanisms of resident macrophage repopulation.

claim: Resident alveolar macrophages undergo in-situ training and maintain an altered phenotype over an extended period.
source: Intriguingly, resident alveolar macrophages (AM) have been shown to undergo in-situ training, maintaining an altered phenotype over an extended period (Zhang et al., 2016; Barth et al., 1995; Keren-Shaul et al., 2019).
evidence: Cited literature demonstrating in-situ training of alveolar macrophages.

claim: CX3CR1+ T cells are implicated in local reprogramming of alveolar macrophages via IFNγ release.
source: One mechanism driving this training in-situ in AMs involves CX3CR1+ T cells, which have been implicated in local reprogramming via IFNγ release.
evidence: Cited literature describing mechanism of alveolar macrophage training.

claim: Interferon-driven responses occur across the organism around three weeks after BCG vaccination, resulting in viral and mycobacterial protection.
source: This process has been demonstrated to occur around three weeks after initial BCG vaccination, after which interferon-driven responses occur across the organism, including lung and BM, resulting in viral and mycobacterial protection.
evidence: Cited literature describing temporal dynamics and outcomes of BCG-induced interferon responses.

claim: Intraperitoneal injection of BCG rapidly delivers the bacteria to target lymphatic organs such as the spleen.
source: To induce tissue specific TI, we used a model of intraperitoneal (i.p.) injection of BCG, which rapidly delivers the bacteria to target lymphatic organs (e.g., spleen), and measured protection against subsequent Salmonella Typhimurium (S.Tm) challenge.
evidence: Description of experimental model and rationale.

claim: An initial depletion of resident red-pulp macrophages is followed by repopulation by recruited trained monocytes and a local self-renewing population.
source: We demonstrate that an initial depletion of resident red-pulp macrophages is followed by repopulation by recruited trained monocytes and a local self-renewing population, contributing to the maintenance of STAT1 signatures and long-lasting protection within the tissue.
evidence: Summary of findings from lineage tracing and gene expression experiments.

claim: Early inhibition of STAT1 activation reduces both RPM loss and recruitment of trained monocytes.
source: Early inhibition of STAT1 activation, using specific JAK-STAT inhibitors, reduces both RPM loss and recruitment of trained monocytes.
evidence: Summary of findings from inhibitor experiments.

claim: There is a temporal window soon after BCG vaccination in which STAT1-dependent activation of long-lived resident cells mediates localized protection.
